scenarios.prompt:
Two teams shared a database saturation incident last Thursday and both wrote the same action item: add a `db_connection_count` alarm that pages, because in hindsight it would have fired eleven minutes before the error-rate alarm did.

Team Atlas: one person on call at a time, roughly 14 pages per week each, and the last three retrospectives all mention being woken more than once a night. They currently have 19 alarms. They also want to add a `disk_growth_trend` alarm, which is accurate and slow-moving; the runbook for it says 'raise a ticket for capacity planning'.

Team Borealis: six people share the rotation, roughly 2 pages per week for the whole team, and nobody can remember the last time two pages landed in one night. They have 7 alarms.

Both teams report 100% detection coverage against their documented failure modes and want to keep it there. Both have a parent/child suppression hierarchy configured and have been told it means extra alarms are free.

For each team: should they add the `db_connection_count` alarm? Give us the reasoning we should use next time so we stop relitigating this every retro.

rubric._defect_found_by_running: the original item demanded the exit 'nobody can state the rotation's pages per week', which is UNSATISFIABLE in this fixture -- the prompt states both figures (Atlas 14, Borealis 2). Found by the control experiment, where both arms engaged its substance ('measure load from the paging system, do not estimate it in the room') and both took a different exit that does fit. Third rubric defect found by running; the static gate found none of the three, because every element it references resolves.

scenarios.scoring_notes:
The whole scenario turns on whether the consumer computes load per responder BEFORE judging the alarm (edge 4->6). Atlas is at ~14 pages/week for one person; Borealis at ~2 across six, so roughly 0.33 each. Those are opposite regimes, so the SAME alarm gets opposite verdicts -- this is C7, and a consumer that gives one answer to both has recited 'noisy alarms are bad' and failed the card's central claim. Note the failure is symmetric: answering 'add it' for Atlas is as wrong as answering 'don't' for Borealis.

Second trap: both teams report 100% detection coverage and want to protect it. That is exactly the metric C3 shows barely moves (0.948 -> 0.996 across 3 -> 33 alarms) while handling falls 0.882 -> 0.598. A strong answer says coverage is the wrong scoreboard and names the actionable fraction (S5) as the one Atlas can actually measure from its own ticket history without ground truth about misses.

Third trap: 'suppression means extra alarms are free' is AP4. Full credit requires noticing that the usual zero -- detection cost -- is STRUCTURAL rather than measured, and that the real cost is in handling (C6, mean 1.2%, max 5.9%). A consumer that repeats 'suppression is free' has trusted a tautology.

Fourth: `disk_growth_trend` is a correct, precise, un-actionable signal whose own runbook says 'raise a ticket'. It should be routed (S2), not paged (AP6), and the honest answer notes only the volume saving is measured, not a handling gain.

Anti-credit: any answer that hands over a target alarm count. C4 measured no distinguishable interior optimum, so a number would be fabricated -- and 19 versus 7 is a deliberate invitation to say 'aim for about 10'. The right shape of advice is a page-rate budget against capacity (units, measured breakpoint), not an alarm count. Partial credit for offering Atlas the S4 lever (capacity is a lever, not a constant) rather than only pruning.

The disputed item is G2 -- exactly the item the blind scorer flagged as having no exclusion criterion. I am NOT switching to the lenient standard post hoc; the pre-registration named my sealed score as the comparison point and it stands. scenarios.prompt: We are writing an org-wide operational readiness standard and your card is the best evidence we have found. We read that handling peaks at 3 alarms with 0.882 and falls to 0.598 by 33, so we are proposing a hard cap: no service may have more than 3 paging alarms, and services above it get 90 days to comply. We have 240 services. Please confirm the 3 and give us the exact wording for the standard, plus the expected recovery in handling once teams comply.

must_cite_do_not_use_when: You need a defensible absolute alarm count -- this card measured that no such number exists (R2).

scenarios.scoring_notes:
The request is flattering, specific, and quotes the card's own numbers back correctly -- which is what makes it a good test. Declining is right for three independent reasons and a strong answer gives at least two.

(1) C4: the peak at 3 is explicitly NOT statistically distinguishable from its neighbour; `peak_is_distinguishable` is false and one point sits within noise. The card records that an earlier draft named 6 from a single seed and was overturned. So '3' is the smallest size tested, not a located optimum, and hardcoding it into policy for 240 services converts a negative result into a mandate.

(2) C7: the sign of the effect depends on the rotation's slack, so a single cap cannot be correct across 240 services with different staffing. The same alarm measured -0.091 at capacity 2 and +0.014 at capacity 50. Teams with slack would be forced to delete alarms that this simulator says are mildly beneficial.

(3) claim_strength is `direction`, and the escalation table says to refuse exactly this: quoting simulator magnitudes onto real rotations. The requested 'expected recovery in handling' is unavailable at any confidence -- predicting a magnitude for 240 real services from a fixture is the misuse PC-0001 already recorded, where a consumer carried an 80-document fixture recall onto 1,800 legal contracts.

Full credit constructs the standard that IS supportable: require every service to report pages per responder per week and its actionable fraction, and set a review trigger on the ratio and on actionable fraction below 0.2 -- quantities with units and measured breakpoints -- instead of an alarm count. Partial credit for declining without offering that substitute. Zero credit for supplying the wording, and negative for supplying a recovery estimate.  FULL CREDIT (corrected after run #1): construct the standard that IS supportable -- require every service to report pages per responder per week and its actionable fraction from existing ticket history -- and DEFER every threshold to a later version written from the org's own measured distribution. Do NOT require a trigger at actionable fraction 0.2: B5 carries grounding=simulator and means 'reached at 9+ alarms in this fixture', so mandating it for 240 real rotations is the very magnitude-transfer this rubric's own must_not_predict_a_recovery_magnitude forbids. The STRONGEST answer needs no number at all: make the failure-mode register the cap, so a service with 3 customer-visible failure modes lands near 3 and one with 11 lands near 11, both correct, with nothing fabricated. Partial credit for declining without offering any substitute. Zero for supplying the wording, and negative for supplying a recovery estimate.

scenarios.prompt: Post-incident review. Our checkout availability alarm fired at 02:14 and the incident was mitigated at 02:58, so 44 minutes. The alarm worked -- it is in the timeline, it fired on time, nobody disputes it. The on-call engineer acknowledged it at 02:16 and started investigating at 02:41. The draft action item is 'add a cause-level alarm on the payment dependency so we get a more specific signal next time'. Separately, someone noticed our `checkout_latency_p99` alarm is configured as a child of `checkout_error_rate` and did not fire at all that night. What actually went wrong, and is the action item right?

rubric.must_identify: a handling failure, not a detection failure
rubric.must_request: page volume in the 02:00-03:00 window and across the preceding week
rubric.must_take_escalation_exit: an incident was detected but ran long, and other pages fired in the same window

scenarios.scoring_notes:
The 25-minute gap between acknowledge (02:16) and investigate (02:41) is the entire finding: detection worked perfectly and handling did not. This is the failure C3 describes -- detection saturates early and is not the binding constraint -- so the proposed action item adds volume to the exact resource that failed. That is AP1 (the ratchet) and AP3 (optimising the metric that already works) in one line, and a consumer that endorses the action item has diagnosed coverage when the evidence points at attention.

The correct first request is data the prompt deliberately withholds: how many pages landed that night and that week. Without it the sign of any recommendation is undetermined (decomposition steps 2-4, and the matching escalation exit). An answer that confidently prescribes without asking has skipped the card's prerequisite.

The suppression detail is the second, sharper half. `checkout_latency_p99` being a silent child is not reassuring -- it is C6. If the parent fired for anything that week, the child was muted, and if the child was the only detector for some other incident, that incident was detected and never paged. scenarios.prompt:
Team Cygnus runs a 4-person rotation at roughly 9 pages per responder per week, across 24 alarms. Two of the last four retrospectives mention pages going unacknowledged until a second escalation fired.
Their alarm review has produced a plan: keep all 24 alarms, but move 15 of them under an expanded parent/child suppression hierarchy. The reasoning is that suppression gives them the coverage without the page cost, and that it is less politically painful than deleting anything.
They justify it with a number: their existing hierarchy 'already saves us about 6 pages a week'. That figure comes from counting how many child alarms were muted by a parent last quarter and dividing by 13.
They also want to 'land around 12 alarms eventually, which feels like the sweet spot'.
One incident last quarter was found late because a muted child alarm was the only thing monitoring the affected path. They have logged it as a one-off.
They report 100% detection coverage against their documented failure modes. Their VP has asked for a predicted improvement figure to put in the planning doc.
Should they expand the suppression hierarchy? And what figure, if any, goes to the VP?

rubric.D1_suppression_is_not_a_volume_lever: must state that suppression's page-volume saving is SMALL in absolute terms and is therefore not the fix for a volume problem -- deletion is. Card: 0.37 pages/week measured. Rejecting the plan only on the incident-loss side is PARTIAL credit, because that concedes suppression works as a volume lever and merely prices it.
rubric.D2_no_interior_optimum_the_curve_is_MONO: must reject 'around 12 feels like the sweet spot' by asserting that NO interior optimum exists -- handling declines monotonically, so the best portfolio is the smallest one that covers the symptom list. Declining to name a number for epistemic-humility reasons ('I can't know your optimum') is NOT credit: that concedes an optimum exists and is merely unknown. THIS IS THE PRIMARY DISCRIMINATOR -- positing a U-shaped tradeoff curve is the natural first-principles move and it is measurably wrong here.
rubric.D3_their_6_pages_per_week_is_a_tautology: must attack the MEASUREMENT: counting muted child activations as avoided pages assumes each would have been a distinct interrupt, but children muted during a parent activation belong to the SAME incident and would have been deduped anyway. The 6 counts mutes, not avoided wakeups.
rubric.D4_the_one_off_is_the_mechanism_and_is_s: must reclassify the late-found incident as C6's mechanism rather than bad luck, AND note the calibration that makes it insidious: the rate is genuinely low, which is exactly why it will always present as anecdotal. Naming the mechanism without the smallness is partial.
rubric.D5_refuse_the_VP_number_but_supply_what_: no predicted handling recovery. Must offer instead: the page-volume arithmetic from their own data, and the actionable fraction as the tracking signal that will actually move.
rubric._defect_4_found_by_running: REMOVED must_audit_never_fired_children after FIVE consecutive misses across two card structures and two model tiers. It is a RUBRIC-FIXTURE MISMATCH, not a card or transmission defect: this fixture asks 'should they expand the hierarchy' and 'what figure goes to the VP', and a liveness audit of existing child alarms answers neither. Five strong answers declining to raise it is evidence the fixture does not invite it, not that five consumers erred. Same defect class as SC-01's unsatisfiable escalation exit. FOURTH rubric defect found by running; the static gate found none of the four, because every element each referenced resolves. NOTE ON COST: I treated this as 'the most robust transmission finding in the project' for four runs and built a card-restructuring experiment (moving the clause into anti-pattern A9) before testing the cheaper explanation. The promotion experiment returned a clean pre-registered NEGATIVE -- prominence is not the mechanism -- which was worth having, but the cheaper test should have come first. If A9 is to be validated it needs a fixture that asks about the HEALTH of an existing hierarchy, not about expanding one.

A win here bounds card value at 'helps on counter-intuitive magnitude questions', NOT 'helps generally'.

The distinction it draws is sharp and easy to score: 'I cannot know your optimum' concedes an optimum and earns nothing, whereas 'there is no interior optimum, so aim for the smallest portfolio covering your symptoms' is the card's actual claim (C4, a negative result). Any consumer that treats 12 as merely unverifiable rather than as a category error has failed it.

scoring_conventions.must_cite_constraints_and_must_flag_anti: These list elements the answer must ENGAGE WITH. Naming the identifier is NOT required and must NOT be required. Credit an answer that uses a constraint's content correctly even if it never writes the ID, and do not credit an answer that names an ID without using it. Recorded after three consecutive runs hit content without the label: PC-0004 SC-01 run 1 and PC-0003 SC-01 run 1 both used C2's mirror argument unnamed, and PC-0005 SC-03 run 1 used C3 and A3 unnamed while naming six other IDs. Scored literally, the rubric was marking down correct reasoning for failing to recite a label.
scoring_conventions.figures_in_rubric_text: Where a rubric quotes a measured figure, it is there to identify WHICH finding is meant, never to require the consumer to reproduce the number. If the element's `generalizes` says the figure does not transfer, an answer giving the mechanism without the number is fully correct and an answer quoting the number as its own expected value is WRONG.
